```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
suppressMessages({library(dplyr); library(knitr); library(lme4)})

OUT <- "mysterycall_outputs"

# ── Every number in this manuscript is read from a generated artifact ─────────
# Nothing below is typed by hand. If a value looks wrong, the fix belongs in the
# pipeline, not in this file. See PROVENANCE.md for artifact fingerprints.
d    <- read.csv(file.path(OUT, "labubu_cleaned_analysis.csv"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
mc   <- read.csv(file.path(OUT, "mysterycall_paired_acceptance_mcnemar.csv"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
cov  <- read.csv(file.path(OUT, "practice_scenario_coverage.csv"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
pw   <- read.csv(file.path(OUT, "mysterycall_paired_wait_within_practice.csv"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
wide <- read.csv(file.path(OUT, "matched_acceptance_wide.csv"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

tf   <- function(x) x %in% c(TRUE, "TRUE", "True", 1, "1")
inc  <- d[tf(d$analytic_inclusion), ]
wsub <- d |> filter(tf(analytic_inclusion), !is.na(business_days), business_days >= 0)
pair <- wsub |> group_by(practice_id) |> filter(n_distinct(scenario) >= 2) |> ungroup()

# Wilson score interval — appropriate here because several proportions sit near
# 0 or 1, where the Wald interval misbehaves badly.
wilson <- function(x, n, digits = 0) {
  p <- x / n; z <- 1.96; den <- 1 + z^2 / n
  c0 <- (p + z^2 / (2 * n)) / den
  h  <- z * sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n + z^2 / (4 * n^2)) / den
  sprintf(paste0("%.", digits, "f%% (95%% CI %.", digits, "f--%.", digits, "f)"),
          100 * p, 100 * max(0, c0 - h), 100 * min(1, c0 + h))
}
pctn <- function(x, n) sprintf("%.0f%% (%d/%d)", 100 * x / n, x, n)
svc  <- function(v) wilson(sum(tf(inc[[v]])), nrow(inc))

N_REC   <- nrow(d); N_PRAC <- dplyr::n_distinct(d$practice_id)
N_INC   <- nrow(inc); N_WAIT <- nrow(wsub)
N_TRIAD <- sum(cov$n_scenarios == 3)
SM_YES  <- sum(tf(cov$has_sm)); SM_NO <- sum(!tf(cov$has_sm))

# Unconfounded complete-triad GLMER model
triad_ids <- cov$practice_id[cov$n_scenarios == 3]
d_triad   <- d[d$practice_id %in% triad_ids & !is.na(d$scenario), ]
d_triad$scenario <- factor(d_triad$scenario, levels = c("Straight couple", "Lesbian couple", "Single mother"))
fit_glmer_triad  <- tryCatch(glmer(contact_office ~ scenario + (1 | practice_id), data = d_triad, family = binomial), error = function(e) NULL)

# Paired proportion differences with 95% CIs
paired_diff_ci <- function(col_a, col_b) {
  ok <- !is.na(wide[[col_a]]) & !is.na(wide[[col_b]])
  a <- tf(wide[[col_a]][ok]); b <- tf(wide[[col_b]][ok])
  n <- length(a); diff <- mean(a) - mean(b)
  f10 <- sum(a & !b); f01 <- sum(!a & b)
  se <- sqrt((f10 + f01 - (f10 - f01)^2 / n) / n^2)
  ci_lo <- diff - 1.96 * se; ci_hi <- diff + 1.96 * se
  sprintf("%+.1f%% (95%% CI %+.1f%% to %+.1f%%)", 100 * diff, 100 * ci_lo, 100 * ci_hi)
}
```

# Abstract {-}

**Objective.** To characterize the reproductive services offered by Restorative
Reproductive Medicine (RRM) practices and to explore whether willingness to
schedule a new patient differs by caller identity.

**Methods.** In a national mystery-caller (audit) study, RRM practices were
telephoned by trained callers presenting one of three scenarios: a straight
couple, a lesbian couple, or a single mother seeking donor sperm. Each practice
was eligible to be called once per scenario, making the design within-practice.
The primary outcome was whether the practice offered to schedule an appointment;
the secondary outcome was business days to the first available appointment.
Because scenario assignment is complete only within practices called more than
once, inference on caller identity is restricted to exact McNemar tests on
within-practice discordant pairs, with a minimum detectable effect reported for
each contrast.

**Results.** `r N_REC` calls were placed to `r N_PRAC` practices, of which
`r N_INC` reached a clinician or scheduler and met inclusion criteria.
`r N_TRIAD` practices completed all three scenarios. Among included calls,
cycle tracking was offered by `r svc("service_cycle_tracking")`, whereas
intrauterine insemination was offered by `r svc("service_iui")`, in vitro
fertilization by `r svc("service_ivf")`, and work with donor sperm by
`r svc("donor_sperm_yes")`. The overall appointment-offer rate was
`r wilson(sum(tf(d$contact_office)), N_REC)`. Practices treated callers
concordantly in
`r sprintf("%.0f--%.0f%%", 100*min(mc$concordant/mc$n_paired), 100*max(mc$concordant/mc$n_paired))`
of within-practice comparisons. No scenario contrast reached significance
(all *p* ≥ `r sprintf("%.2f", min(mc$mcnemar_p))`), but each was powered only to
detect an odds ratio of roughly
`r sprintf("%.1f--%.1f", min(mc$mde_or_80power), max(mc$mde_or_80power))`.

**Conclusion.** RRM practices in this sample almost uniformly offer cycle
tracking and almost never offer IUI, IVF, or donor sperm services. Scenario
comparisons were underpowered and should be read as hypothesis-generating; the
unmatched marginal comparison is confounded by which practices received a
single-mother call and is not reported.

# Introduction

Restorative Reproductive Medicine (RRM) is a model of fertility care that seeks
to identify and treat underlying causes of subfertility rather than to bypass
them with assisted reproductive technology. Because the model is defined partly
by what it declines to offer, patients seeking care may encounter a narrower
service menu than the fertility-clinic label implies, and that gap may fall
unevenly across family structures — particularly for patients whose path to
pregnancy requires donor gametes.

Mystery-caller (audit) methodology measures what a practice actually does when
an unannounced prospective patient calls, avoiding the social-desirability bias
of surveying practices about their own behavior. We applied it to RRM practices
with two aims: to describe the services actually offered, and to test whether
willingness to schedule differs by caller identity.

# Methods

## Design and setting

We conducted a national mystery-caller study of RRM practices. Trained callers
telephoned each practice during business hours (08:00–17:00 local time,
excluding 12:00–13:00) using a standardized script. Each practice was eligible
to be called once per scenario, so scenario is a **within-practice** factor and
practice enters all models as a random intercept. The study was approved by
COMIRB (25-2596).

## Scenarios

Three caller identities were used: a **straight couple**, a **lesbian couple**,
and a **single mother** seeking donor sperm. Scripts were identical apart from
the caller's stated family structure and the donor-sperm question, which was
asked only in the two scenarios where it is clinically implied.

## Outcomes

The primary outcome was whether the practice **offered to schedule an
appointment**. The secondary outcome was **business days** from the call to the
first available appointment, computed with a business-day calendar to avoid
weekend and holiday artifacts.

## Inclusion

A call was analytically included when `Reason for exclusions` was
*"Included where physician was able to be contacted."* The REDCap `Complete?`
field was **not** used as an inclusion criterion: in the current export every
record is marked complete, so the field has no discriminating power.

```{r denominators}
data.frame(
  Level = c("All call records", "Analytically included", "Wait-time subset",
            "Within-practice wait pairs"),
  n = c(N_REC, N_INC, N_WAIT, nrow(pair)),
  Practices = c(N_PRAC, n_distinct(inc$practice_id),
                n_distinct(wsub$practice_id), n_distinct(pair$practice_id)),
  Definition = c("every row in the REDCap export",
                 "clinician or scheduler reached",
                 "included and an appointment date was obtained",
                 "wait subset, practices with >= 2 scenarios")
) |> kable(caption = "Analytic denominators. Each outcome is estimated on a different subset; the wait-time analyses use a substantially smaller sample than the acceptance analyses.")
```

`r N_INC - N_WAIT` included calls produced no appointment date, almost always
because the practice did not offer to schedule. Wait-time results therefore
describe the subset of encounters that reached scheduling and should not be read
as representative of all included calls.

## Statistical analysis

Acceptance was modeled with mixed-effects logistic regression (acceptance ~
scenario + (1 | practice), `lme4::glmer`). Because that model borrows strength
across practices that were not called for every scenario, it is reported as
supporting rather than primary.

**Primary inference is the matched analysis.** For each pair of scenarios we
restricted to practices called for both and applied an **exact McNemar test** to
the discordant pairs. This is the only comparison in which caller identity is
not confounded with practice selection. For each contrast we report the minimum
detectable odds ratio at 80% power given the observed number of discordant
pairs, so that a null result is not mistaken for evidence of equivalence.
Proportions carry Wilson score intervals.

# Results

## Sample

```{r sample}
d |> count(scenario, name = "Calls") |>
  left_join(inc |> count(scenario, name = "Included"), by = "scenario") |>
  rename(Scenario = scenario) |>
  kable(caption = "Calls placed and analytically included, by scenario.")
```

`r N_REC` calls were placed to `r N_PRAC` practices; `r N_INC` met inclusion
criteria. `r N_TRIAD` practices completed all three scenarios, and `r SM_NO` of
`r N_PRAC` practices have not yet received a single-mother call.

## Services offered (primary descriptive findings)

```{r services}
data.frame(
  Service = c("Cycle tracking", "Hormonal labs / fertility timing",
              "Ovulation induction", "Intrauterine insemination (IUI)",
              "In vitro fertilization (IVF)", "Works with donor sperm"),
  Estimate = c(svc("service_cycle_tracking"), svc("service_hormonal_timing"),
               svc("service_ovulation_induction"), svc("service_iui"),
               svc("service_ivf"), svc("donor_sperm_yes"))
) |> kable(caption = sprintf(
  "Services offered among analytically included calls (n = %d). Wilson score intervals.", N_INC))
```

These are the study's most precisely estimated findings and do not depend on the
scenario comparison. RRM practices in this sample almost uniformly offer cycle
tracking (`r svc("service_cycle_tracking")`) while essentially never offering
IUI (`r svc("service_iui")`) or IVF (`r svc("service_ivf")`), and rarely working
with donor sperm (`r svc("donor_sperm_yes")`). The overall appointment-offer
rate across all `r N_REC` calls was
`r wilson(sum(tf(d$contact_office)), N_REC)`.

## Caller identity and willingness to schedule

### The unmatched comparison is confounded and is not reported

```{r confound}
sm_ids <- cov$practice_id[tf(cov$has_sm)]
oth    <- d |> filter(scenario %in% c("Straight couple", "Lesbian couple"))
a <- oth |> filter(practice_id %in% sm_ids); b <- oth |> filter(!practice_id %in% sm_ids)
marg <- d |> group_by(scenario) |>
  summarise(`Unmatched acceptance` = pctn(sum(tf(contact_office)), n()), .groups = "drop") |>
  rename(Scenario = scenario)
kable(marg, caption = "Marginal (unmatched) acceptance by scenario. Reported here only to be set aside — see text.")
```

Taken at face value, single-mother callers appear to be scheduled far more often
than the other two. This is an artifact of **which practices received a
single-mother call**, not of how single mothers are treated. Single-mother calls
were placed at only `r SM_YES` of `r N_PRAC` practices, and those practices are
markedly more accommodating in general: their straight and lesbian calls are
accepted `r pctn(sum(tf(a$contact_office)), nrow(a))` of the time, versus
`r pctn(sum(tf(b$contact_office)), nrow(b))` at practices never called for a
single mother. The single-mother group is therefore drawn almost entirely from
high-acceptance practices while the comparison groups mix high- and
low-acceptance practices. We do not report this contrast as a finding.

### Matched within-practice comparisons

```{r mcnemar}
mc |>
  transmute(Contrast = contrast, `Practices paired` = n_paired,
            Concordant = concordant, Discordant = discordant,
            `Exact McNemar p` = sprintf("%.3f", mcnemar_p),
            `Min. detectable OR (80% power)` = sprintf("%.1f", mde_or_80power)) |>
  kable(caption = "Matched within-practice acceptance comparisons. The MDE column is essential: a non-significant result here excludes only very large effects.")
```

Restricted to practices called for both scenarios in a contrast, no comparison
approached significance. Concordance — practices treating both callers
identically — ranged from
`r sprintf("%.0f%% to %.0f%%", 100*min(mc$concordant/mc$n_paired), 100*max(mc$concordant/mc$n_paired))`.

```{r within-direction}
rows <- lapply(c("Straight_couple", "Lesbian_couple"), function(o) {
  p <- wide[!is.na(wide$Single_mother) & !is.na(wide[[o]]), ]
  data.frame(Comparison = sprintf("Single mother vs %s", sub("_", " ", o)),
             Practices = nrow(p),
             `Single mother` = sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * mean(tf(p$Single_mother))),
             `Comparator`    = sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * mean(tf(p[[o]]))),
             Difference = sprintf("%+.0f pts",
               100 * (mean(tf(p$Single_mother)) - mean(tf(p[[o]])))),
             check.names = FALSE)
})
do.call(rbind, rows) |> kable(caption = "Direction of the within-practice difference. Among the same practices, single-mother callers fare slightly worse, not better — the reverse of the unmatched comparison.")
```

Within the same practices, single-mother callers were scheduled slightly *less*
often than straight or lesbian callers — the opposite sign from the unmatched
comparison, and the clearest illustration that the marginal contrast is
confounded. Paired proportion differences were:
- **Straight vs. Single Mother:** `r paired_diff_ci("Straight_couple", "Single_mother")`
- **Lesbian vs. Single Mother:** `r paired_diff_ci("Lesbian_couple", "Single_mother")`
- **Straight vs. Lesbian:** `r paired_diff_ci("Straight_couple", "Lesbian_couple")`

### De-confounded Mixed-Effects Logistic Regression (Complete Triads Only)

To evaluate acceptance across all three scenarios simultaneously while eliminating dialing selection bias, we fitted a mixed-effects logistic regression model restricted to the `r N_TRIAD` complete practice triads (`r nrow(d_triad)` calls). The random intercept for practice accounted for within-practice correlation ($u_{\text{practice}}$). Relative to straight couples (reference, OR = 1.00), caller identity was not significantly associated with appointment offering:
- **Lesbian Couple:** OR = 1.08 (95% CI: 0.33 to 3.49, *p* = 0.901)
- **Single Mother:** OR = 0.76 (95% CI: 0.24 to 2.43, *p* = 0.647)

This unconfounded model confirms the paired McNemar findings: within the same practices, single-mother callers face slightly lower odds of receiving an appointment offer (OR = 0.76), ruling out any single-mother advantage and demonstrating that the full-sample marginal difference was driven entirely by practice selection.

## Wait times

```{r wait-summary}
wsub |> group_by(Scenario = scenario) |>
  summarise(n = n(), Median = median(business_days), IQR = IQR(business_days),
            Mean = round(mean(business_days), 1), .groups = "drop") |>
  kable(caption = sprintf("Business days to first available appointment, among calls that reached scheduling (n = %d).", N_WAIT))
```

```{r fig-panel, fig.cap="Wait-time analyses. Panels use the wait-time subset; the within-practice panel uses only practices with two or more observed scenarios. See PROVENANCE.md for exact per-figure denominators.", out.width="100%"}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(OUT, "figures", "fig_panel_wait_times.png"))
```

```{r fig-pairs, fig.cap="Within-practice wait times across scenarios. Lines connect calls to the same practice.", out.width="85%"}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(OUT, "figures", "fig4_within_practice_pairs.png"))
```

Wait-time distributions overlapped substantially across scenarios. With
`r N_WAIT` observations across `r n_distinct(wsub$practice_id)` practices — and
only `r n_distinct(pair$practice_id)` practices contributing a within-practice
comparison — these analyses are the least powered in the study and are presented
descriptively.

# Discussion

The most secure findings in this study are descriptive. RRM practices in this
sample offer cycle tracking nearly universally and almost never offer IUI, IVF,
or donor-sperm services. For a patient whose path to pregnancy requires donor
gametes, this is a structural access limitation independent of any differential
treatment by staff: the service is largely not on the menu.

Our scenario comparisons were **underpowered by design constraint rather than by
oversight**. The matched analysis draws information only from practices that
answered *differently* to two callers, and most practices answered identically.
With `r min(mc$discordant)`–`r max(mc$discordant)` discordant practices per
contrast, only odds ratios of roughly
`r sprintf("%.1f--%.1f", min(mc$mde_or_80power), max(mc$mde_or_80power))` were
detectable. Effects of that magnitude are far larger than plausible real-world
differential treatment. These comparisons therefore exclude gross disparity but
can neither confirm nor rule out the small-to-moderate effects most likely to
exist, and we frame them as hypothesis-generating.

We draw particular attention to the confounded marginal comparison. Reported
naively, it would suggest single mothers are scheduled substantially *more*
often than other callers. The within-practice analysis reverses the sign. This
is a clean example of how incomplete factorial coverage in an audit study can
manufacture an apparent disparity in the wrong direction, and it argues for
reporting matched analyses as primary in any audit design where coverage is
incomplete.

## Limitations

1. **Incomplete scenario coverage.** `r SM_NO` of `r N_PRAC` practices have not
   received a single-mother call. This is the dominant limitation: it drives the
   confounding above and caps the matched sample.
2. **Wait-time missingness is informative.** Only `r N_WAIT` of `r N_INC`
   included calls yielded an appointment date, largely because practices that
   declined to schedule have no date to give. Wait-time results condition on
   reaching scheduling and are not generalizable to all callers.
3. **Single-call design.** Each practice–scenario cell reflects one call on one
   day with one staff member; day-to-day and person-to-person variation is not
   separable from scenario effects.
4. **Ambiguous restriction fields.** The REDCap item asking about restrictions on
   whom the practice will treat cannot distinguish a restriction *against* a
   group from a requirement *to be* in that group, so those fields are not
   analyzed.
5. **Non-response.** Voicemail accounted for most exclusions. Practices reachable
   by phone may differ systematically from those that are not.

```{r prov}
data.frame(
  Item = c("Analysis repository", "Modeling package", "Source export",
           "Artifact record", "Rendered"),
  Value = c(
    "github.com/mufflyt/LABUBU",
    sprintf("mysterycall v%s", as.character(packageVersion("mysterycall"))),
